title: TSM Stock at 21x After a 30% Chip Sell-Off [2026] - shattered.io
content: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, the company behind the NYSE ticker TSM, is the stock a Motley Fool columnist would buy and hold after a brutal stretch for chip shares. In a column syndicated on Yahoo Finance and headlined “Not Nvidia. Not Micron. After the Chip Sell-Off, I’d Buy This AI Stock and Hold It Forever.”, the author argues that TSM stock offers a better deal than the two names that dominated the AI trade. Listings show the piece ran on November 7, 2026. The timing matters. The PHLX Semiconductor Sector index sits roughly 30% below where it stood on October 6, Nvidia is down 21%, and Micron is down 34%. TSMC trades near 21 times forward earnings, while Micron changes hands at about 4 times. Compare that to Apple’s 36x forward earnings, and a 21x multiple on the company that builds the world’s most advanced AI processors starts to look like a real debate rather than a throwaway pick. This analysis walks through the numbers behind the call, tests the thesis against the obvious objections, and sorts what is confirmed from what is opinion. Nothing here is investment advice. The “hold it forever” framing belongs to the Motley Fool columnist, and no price target appears in the verified material. The week's biggest stories in tech, gaming and security, in one email. Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions. Start with the damage from the semiconductor sell-off. According to the research behind this story, the PHLX Semiconductor Sector index is down approximately 30% since October 6. That index tracks the biggest US-listed chip designers, equipment makers, and manufacturers, so a drop of that size is a sector-wide event rather than one company’s bad quarter. Nvidia, which trades as NVDA on Nasdaq, fell about 21% from its October 6 record close in the period the column cites. A separate market update put the slide at 21.96%. Micron, ticker MU, took a bigger hit at roughly 34%. TSMC shares finished the referenced week down 7.61%, which is a smaller loss than either of the stocks the columnist passed over. Outlets covering the move frame it as a question of whether the AI buildout can keep its pace. Upside asked whether the good times are over for AI stocks, and our own earlier report on the $2.5 trillion AI sell-off and its four triggers traced how political risk fed the rout. The comparison table later in this piece collects the confirmed figures side by side. The column’s logic is a picks-and-shovels argument. Every company designing an advanced AI accelerator needs someone to manufacture it, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing is the largest third-party chip foundry on the planet. If Nvidia, AMD, or a hyperscaler’s in-house team wins the next design contest, the wafers still run through TSMC fabs. That structure explains why the columnist treats the foundry as the safer way to own the AI chip stocks theme. A designer can lose share to a rival. A foundry that makes chips for all the rivals collects revenue either way. The column also notes that TSMC’s forward multiple of about 21 sits close to Nvidia’s, so buyers do not pay a steep premium for the lower design risk. Be clear about what this argument is. It is a stock pick from a financial-media columnist, published the day after a sector-wide drop. The Motley Fool is known for long-horizon, buy-and-hold advice, so a “hold forever” label fits the house style. Readers should weigh the reasoning and the data, then decide for themselves whether any of it applies to their own portfolio. The strongest number in the thesis is TSMC’s foundry market share, and it explains most of the column’s confidence. According to the research, the company captures 73% of contract semiconductor-manufacturing spending. Put plainly, of every $100 that chip designers spend to have someone else build their processors, about $73 goes to TSMC. That concentration cuts both ways. For investors it signals pricing power and a customer base that cannot easily switch, because moving a leading-edge design to another fab takes years of engineering work. For the industry it creates a single point of failure. A fab outage, a regional shock, or a trade restriction would ripple through nearly every major AI product at once. The market has priced the dependence in for years, and the semiconductor sell-off did not change it. What changed is the multiple that investors will pay for chip exposure. When the SOX index loses a third of its value from a peak, the question shifts from “who is growing fastest” to “who owns the part of the chain that does not go away.” Beyond that foundry market share, TSMC also serves a second business that gets less attention. Its mature-node fabs, which the company’s earnings materials describe in terms of 180 nm and 90 nm processes, supply power-management chips used in AI data centers. Those parts are cheap next to a flagship accelerator, but a server rack cannot run without them. TSMC backs its position with spending. The company raised its 2026 capital budget to $60 billion to $64 billion, according to its second-quarter 2026 earnings call transcript on the investor relations site. In 2025 the company spent $40.9 billion, and in 2024 it spent $29.8 billion. Run the arithmetic and the scale becomes clear. Capex rose about 37% from 2024 to 2025. The 2026 guidance implies a further jump of roughly 47% at the low end and 56% at the high end versus 2025 (my calculation from the reported figures). Few manufacturers of any kind raise their capital budgets by half in a single year. The earnings call also broke the 2026 budget into buckets. About 70% to 80% goes to advanced process technologies, roughly 10% to specialty technologies, and 10% to 20% to advanced packaging, testing, mask making, and related work. On a $60 billion to $64 billion budget, the advanced-process share alone works out to somewhere between $42 billion and $51 billion (again my arithmetic). Those buckets tell you what management thinks the AI cycle needs. Packaging has become a bottleneck for large accelerators, so the 10% to 20% slice deserves attention. If it grows in later years, it would signal that chip assembly, not wafer starts, limits how fast customers can ship. The valuation gap drives the column’s conclusion. TSMC trades at about 21 times forward earnings, a multiple the article describes as similar to Nvidia’s. Micron trades at roughly 4 times. A five-fold difference between two chip stocks, in the same sell-off, begs an explanation. The usual explanation is cyclicality. Memory makers earn peak profits when prices spike and then watch margins collapse when supply catches up. Investors apply a low multiple to peak-looking earnings because they expect those earnings to fall. A foundry with long-term contracts and 73% of its market looks steadier, so buyers pay more per dollar of profit. The columnist chose not to buy Micron despite the cheap multiple, which signals skepticism about earnings durability. Memory pricing has been wild this year. Our report on DDR5 pricing, where a chip that cost $8.70 now sells for $48, shows how hot the market ran. Micron’s own quote page on Robinhood gives readers a place to check the live numbers. A 4x multiple says the market expects profits to drop. If memory prices hold, Micron looks mispriced. If they roll over, 4x was the right call. The Motley Fool column sided with the safer exposure, and the 34% drop shows many investors share that unease. Management commentary supports the demand story, though readers should remember that executives talk up their own business. During the third-quarter earnings call, TSMC Chairman and CEO C.C. Wei said, “All AI players are working with TSMC,” according to CRN Asia’s coverage of the call. The same report quotes him on supply: “The demand remained far above what the company could currently supply.” Earlier in the year Wei described the long-run trend in similar terms. In July he said, “The CAGR is getting stronger and stronger and stronger,” as The Next Platform reported in a piece about how AI chips now drive around a third of TSMC’s revenue. The quote refers to the compound growth rate in the company’s AI-related business. Nvidia’s Jensen Huang has praised the supply chain in public. In a conversation reported by PJFP alongside Lex Fridman, he said, “Nothing gives me more pleasure than last year when my entire supply chain’s stock price went up 300%, mine stayed flat.” The 300% figure is Huang’s own characterization, and this article has not verified it. The remark still shows how Nvidia’s CEO sees the relative winners in the AI buildout. Taken together, these statements describe a company that says it cannot build enough, which is the best possible message for a foundry. They do not guarantee that customers keep ordering at the same pace if AI budgets shrink. A supply-constrained business can turn into an oversupplied one quickly when end demand cools. The sell-off did not stay inside the GPU and memory names. Chips that serve phones, industrial gear, and data centers all felt pressure from the same risk-off mood. We covered the ripple in several earlier pieces, and they paint a mixed picture of where demand holds and where it fades. Microchip guided its next quarter down 1%, and the company pointed to stretching lead times and foundry pricing, as we reported in Microchip Guides Down 1% as Lead Times Stretch. That is a small number, but it comes from a chip company far from the AI spotlight, and it shows foundry capacity still limits parts of the market. Qualcomm showed the split between mobile weakness and data-center promise. The stock fell 9% as handset revenue dropped 26% to $5.14 billion, with data-center revenue of $650 million offering a counterweight. AI exposure helps, but it does not yet offset a slumping phone business at the scale Qualcomm needs. Arm, which licenses designs rather than building chips, guided its next quarter to $1.54 billion, only just above the $1.53 billion analysts expected. For anyone sorting through AI chip stocks, the pattern is clear: companies with direct, capacity-constrained exposure to AI wafers have the strongest story, and those with consumer-device exposure carry the most doubt. The three stocks in the column represent three different bets on the same boom. Nvidia designs the accelerators, Micron supplies the memory that feeds them, and TSMC manufactures the logic. Each faces a different failure mode, which is why the table below sorts them by what could go wrong. AMD sits in the designer camp as well. Our look at the AMD stress test, with $8.5 billion in data-center revenue out of $13.4 billion total, shows the same dynamic. Whoever wins sockets in the next AI generation, TSMC probably builds the winner, and that structural advantage is what the Motley Fool column rewards. TSMC’s recent history reads like a case study in compounding. The company grew sales 35.9% in 2025, according to the figures cited in the research, while it lifted capex from $29.8 billion to $40.9 billion. Growth that fast, funded by heavy reinvestment, is what pushed AI chip stocks to the highs of early October. The sector has seen similar swings before. Chip stocks tend to sell off sharply when investors question the durability of end demand, and then recover once customers confirm their orders. A semiconductor sell-off of roughly 30% in about a month is large, but the real test is whether capex guidance and customer orders hold, not the stock chart alone. What differs this time is the size of the commitments. Hyperscalers have borrowed heavily to fund data centers, and our report on Big Tech bonds pushing US issuance to a $1.88 trillion record shows how much debt now sits behind the buildout. If those buyers pull back, the foundry feels it first because it must order wafers months ahead. For investors, the rout reset expectations. TSMC now trades near 21 times forward earnings, and Micron trades near 4 times. Those are the clearest signals that the market is separating durable businesses from cyclical ones. For hardware buyers, the effects arrive more slowly. Capacity expansion at TSMC takes years, so a $60 billion to $64 billion budget in 2026 lands in products over the following cycles. If the sell-off prompts customers to trim orders, GPU and memory supply could loosen. If it does not, prices for consumer parts could stay high. Our hardware coverage tracks both sides. Data from market pages such as StockAnalysis lets readers check TSM’s price, valuation, and financial history directly. Checking those pages matters more than trusting any single column, since forward multiples move daily and the figures in this article reflect the Motley Fool’s November 7 snapshot. No stock deserves the word “forever” without a list of what could break it. A column that champions one company after a drop should face the same scrutiny as any bull case. The table below sets out how a bull and a bear would read the same facts. The same 73% share that makes TSMC attractive also makes it a target for policy. Export controls, tariffs, and geopolitical tension affect where the company can build and whom it can sell to. The verified material does not quantify those risks, so this article leaves them as open variables instead of guessing at numbers. Capital intensity adds another weight. Spending $60 billion or more in one year only pays off if fabs stay full. A stock priced at 21 times earnings has less room for error than one priced at 4 times, even though the latter carries more cycle risk. These are analytical judgments, not forecasts from the sources, and none is a recommendation. The takeaway: the Motley Fool column makes a structural case, not a timing call. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing builds the chips for most of the AI industry, holds 73% of contract chipmaking spending, and plans to invest $60 billion to $64 billion this year. After a 30% drop in the SOX index, it trades near 21 times forward earnings. Against that, the bear case is real. The stock is not cheap, spending is enormous, and a single supplier carries enormous weight for the whole sector. Anyone considering TSM stock after the semiconductor sell-off should read the company’s own filings, check live prices, and weigh how much concentration they already hold in AI chip stocks. Which stock does the Motley Fool recommend after the chip sell-off? The column names Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, which trades as TSM on the NYSE. It positions the stock as a better buy-and-hold choice than Nvidia or Micron. How far have chip stocks fallen? The PHLX Semiconductor Sector index is down approximately 30% since October 6. Nvidia is down 21% and Micron is down 34% over the period the column cites. How is TSM stock valued? The column puts TSMC at about 21 times forward earnings, similar to Nvidia. Micron trades at roughly 4 times. What is TSMC’s foundry market share? TSMC accounts for 73% of contract semiconductor-manufacturing spending, according to the research cited here. How much will TSMC spend on capital projects in 2026? The company guided to $60 billion to $64 billion, up from $40.9 billion in 2025 and $29.8 billion in 2024. Is this investment advice? No. This is news analysis based on a published column and public data. The “hold forever” view belongs to the columnist, and readers should do their own research before buying any stock. Why does Micron trade at only 4 times earnings? The article does not state the market’s reasoning. A common explanation is memory-cycle risk, where profits peak and then fall as supply catches up, but that is analysis rather than a confirmed fact from the column. Shares of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (NYSE:TSM | TSM Price Prediction) rose 6.26% in U.S. trading on November 6, 2026. The move came one day after a 10.78% drop to $353.10. The catalyst was a report that TSMC recently began drawing up plans to make vertically stacked DRAM at the request of its top customer, NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA). The report cited two people with direct knowledge of the matter. Neither company has confirmed it, and TSMC does not comment on market speculation. The rest of the chip group also rebounded. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (NASDAQ:SMH) rose 3.52%, NVIDIA gained 2.78% to $186.64, and Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) added 5.12%. TSMC’s ADR rose more than the sector, topping out at a 7.7% gain early in the session, but it still finished the week down 7.61%. Taiwan’s market had already closed when the report came out. Nothing has been signed or announced. TSMC is reportedly deciding whether to build new fabs or buy and retool an existing site, similar to Micron’s $1.8 billion purchase of a Powerchip fab in Taiwan in March. The effort is reportedly led by Hsu Kuo-chin, a TSMC vice president who runs advanced packaging and previously ran Micron’s regional operations. Vertically stacked DRAM puts memory cells on top of one another within a single chip. High-bandwidth memory (HBM) is a different product that stacks whole memory chips. TSMC has not said how much it might invest or when production could begin. Its 2026 capital budget is already $60 billion to $64 billion, and a memory fab would add to that. Its supply obligations reached $279.0 billion, mostly for the memory that goes into Vera Rubin, and its CFO said: “The magnitude of the price increase has exceeded our prior expectations.” A second supplier would give NVIDIA more leverage over memory makers, although no new supply would arrive in time to affect results for years. Micron’s gain on Friday shows no sign that the report hurt memory stocks. Its 22.01% weekly loss came from the earlier selloff. Micron also forecasts $61.5 billion in quarterly revenue and is already co-designing HBM4E with NVIDIA. TSMC holds patents on vertical DRAM. Memory has also historically made thinner margins than leading-edge logic, while TSMC posted a 66.4% gross margin last quarter. Building new capacity takes a long time. Micron expects first wafers from its new Idaho fab in mid-calendar 2027 and says meaningful supply growth will take a few more quarters after that. The logic business remains the core of the investment case. TSMC forecasts fourth-quarter revenue of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion, up from $46.72 billion, and expects full-year 2026 growth of about 44%. The memory report is a long-term possibility that isn’t priced into those numbers. Taiwan Semiconductor, the world's largest chip foundry, is considering expanding its business into advanced storage chip manufacturing and has, at the request of its largest customer NVIDIA, begun formulating plans to produce 3D DRAM (three-dimensional dynamic random-access memory). The Zhitong Finance APP has learned that, according to media reports, Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM.US), the world's largest chip foundry, is considering expanding its business into advanced storage chip manufacturing and has, at the request of its largest customer NVIDIA (NVDA.US), begun formulating plans to produce 3D DRAM (three-dimensional dynamic random-access memory). If this plan is ultimately implemented, Taiwan Semiconductor could further expand its influence in the artificial intelligence (AI) hardware supply chain. According to media reports citing two insiders, Taiwan Semiconductor has recently begun studying production plans for 3D DRAM. This move stems from NVIDIA's demand for advanced memory chips and reflects that AI chip designers are actively seeking to diversify their sources of critical components. 3D DRAM is an advanced memory chip technology that employs a three-dimensional architecture, aiming to increase storage density through novel cell layouts and manufacturing processes, while providing more technological options for future high-performance computing systems. For Taiwan Semiconductor, which has long focused on logic chip foundry and advanced packaging, entering advanced DRAM manufacturing would mean further expanding its business portfolio. Currently, Taiwan Semiconductor dominates the global advanced logic chip manufacturing sector and is also a key manufacturing partner for NVIDIA's AI accelerators. If it further enters the advanced memory chip production field in the future, Taiwan Semiconductor will have the opportunity to play a role in more critical segments of AI computing hardware. This potential business expansion comes at a time when the global memory chip market is facing severe supply constraints. As the boom in generative AI and data center construction continues, demand for high-performance computing hardware and associated memory chips is surging, tightening supply and driving prices sharply higher. For AI chip designers such as NVIDIA, memory chips are a critical component that determines the performance and production scale of computing systems. Supply shortages could not only drive up hardware manufacturing costs but also constrain the pace of AI infrastructure deployment. Consequently, major tech companies, including NVIDIA and Apple (AAPL.US), are actively seeking additional sources of memory chip supply to mitigate supply chain risks. The impact of rising storage chip prices has also begun to ripple through the consumer electronics market. Earlier this year, Apple raised the prices of some products, citing higher storage costs, highlighting that the tight supply of storage chips is no longer confined to the AI server sector but is affecting a broader range of electronic product markets. Against this backdrop, NVIDIA is urging Taiwan Semiconductor to research 3D DRAM production, which may help it establish a more diversified advanced storage chip supply system in the future. However, the relevant plans are currently still in the preliminary research and planning stages. The report did not disclose the scale of funding Taiwan Semiconductor plans to invest, its potential production capacity, the mass-production timeline, or whether it will formally launch commercial production in the future. Furthermore, 3D DRAM is not entirely the same technological route as High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), which is widely used in current AI accelerators, and Taiwan Semiconductor's research into 3D DRAM production does not mean it has decided to enter the existing HBM market. title: TSMC Stock (TSM) Falls 10.8% as Chip Stocks Slide (Nov 5) - Gotrade
content: Gotrade News - In the latest TSMC stock news, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) fell 10.78% to close at $353.10 on Thursday, November 5, 2026, as a sell-off in chip stocks ran into a second day. TSMC itself had no news, according to TIKR, which tied the drop in TSMC stock to fears of a slower AI build-out after Democrats' larger-than-expected midterm wins. Regular-session close on Thursday, November 5, 2026, 4:00 p.m. New York time. Stock prices: Yahoo Finance, cross-checked against the closing price on Nasdaq.com. Volume and 30-day average volume: Nasdaq.com. 52-week range: Yahoo Finance daily highs and lows since November 6, 2025. Indices and the 10-year Treasury yield: Yahoo Finance daily closes for the same date. Follow TSM's latest price on our TSMC (TSM) stock price today page. TSM opened below Wednesday's close and sold off through the session, finishing just $1.91 above its intraday low. Trading was heavy, with volume running 282.80% above the stock's average. The drop was steeper than the broader market's. On the same November 5 session, the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% to 24,315.00, the S&P 500 lost 4.36% to 7,353.73 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average slid 3.44% to 51,523.06, leaving TSM 5.26 percentage points behind the Nasdaq. The US 10-year Treasury yield fell 5.7 basis points to 4.84%. Chip peers fell hard as well. Nvidia (NVDA) lost 9.26%, while AMD (AMD) dropped 17.26% and Micron (MU) fell 17.46%. After the decline, TSM sits 27.56% below its 52-week high and 32.34% above its 52-week low. The drop did not come from company news: TIKR reported that TSMC had no news of its own on Thursday. Financial media tied the fall instead to a chip rout that deepened after Democrats' larger-than-expected midterm wins raised fears of a slower AI build-out. Two industry reports added pressure, as reported by TIKR. Qualcomm, a TSMC customer, warned on memory costs after Wednesday's close, and Bloomberg reported on Thursday morning that Micron had paused a $4.5 billion Taiwan plant. The selling also reflects wider doubts about AI budgets. According to The Motley Fool, recent selling pressure has raised questions about the sustainability of massive AI infrastructure spending. The next read on demand is TSMC's October revenue, which TIKR says is due next week and will be the first check on the fourth-quarter guidance.
